parts.title: Enrolling in a salsa class
parts.context: A man phones a dance school to join a salsa class.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a dance school to enrol in a salsa class. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: Casa de Baile Dance School, Marisol speaking.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Hello. I'd like to join a salsa class, please. I'm going to my cousin's wedding abroad, and I'd like to be able to dance at it.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: How exciting. I'll take a few details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller needs to dance at a wedding, so 'wedding' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Dev Mehta. That's M-E-H-T-A.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: Thank you, Dev. And how old are you?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: I'm thirty-one.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: Have you danced before?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: A little. I did some tango a few years ago, but I stopped when I changed jobs.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: That will help, because you'll already know about rhythm and leading. Where is the wedding?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: In Cuba, which is why I'm trying to learn salsa. My cousin says everyone dances there.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: Which evening would suit you?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Tuesdays, if possible. Wednesdays I go to the gym.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: The Tuesday class is for beginners, and it starts at seven in the evening. A term is ten weeks, and it costs sixty pounds.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: That sounds fair. What about the other levels?

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: The Improvers' class is on Wednesday evenings at eight, and also costs sixty pounds. Then we have an Advanced class on Fridays at seven, and that one costs eighty pounds, because it's taught by two instructors.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: I'm sure I'll start with the beginners. Can I try a class first?

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: Yes, we offer a taster class for five pounds, and if you decide to join, that money is taken off the price of the term.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Is there anything I should wear?

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: Comfortable clothes, and shoes with a smooth sole, so that you can turn easily. Trainers are not ideal, because they grip the floor too much.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Do I need a partner?

script.speaker: marisol
script.text: No, we change partners during the lesson, so you'll dance with everyone. See you on Tuesday, Dev.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A street dance festival
parts.context: An organiser describes the programme of a dance festival.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear an organiser describing the programme of a street dance festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: Hello, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information evening about the Riverside Dance Festival. I'm Carmen Lopez, the festival director, and I'll start with the programme.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: On Friday evening, the festival opens with a ballet gala, performed by dancers from the city's ballet school. It's the only ticketed event on Friday, and it takes place in the theatre.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: On Saturday morning, there's a street dance workshop for anyone who'd like to try, with teachers from three local studios. You don't need any experience.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: Saturday afternoon is for folk dances from Asia, performed by groups from five countries, in colourful costumes, and the audience is invited to join in the last dance.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: On Saturday evening, the highlight is the flamenco show, which begins at eight o'clock, and which many people think is the best part of the weekend.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: And on Sunday afternoon, the festival closes with a salsa party, with a live band. Irish step dancing and a tango lesson were planned, but we had to cancel them because of a clash with another event.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: A few facts. This year, twenty-four dance groups are taking part, which is twice as many as last year, and they come from all over the world.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: Most events will be held in the town square, with a big stage in the middle and seats around the edge, but the ballet gala will be in the theatre, as I said.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: A weekend pass costs thirty pounds, which covers all events except the gala. Day tickets are fifteen pounds, and under-sixteens go free.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: If it rains, the events will move to the sports hall, which holds about eight hundred people. We'll announce any change on our website and on the radio.

script.speaker: lopez
script.text: Tickets can be bought online, or at the tourist information office, which is open until the end of the festival. We don't sell them at the door, so please plan ahead.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Social media marketing for a start-up
parts.context: Two business students plan a marketing campaign.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two business students, Priya and Joel, planning social media marketing for a start-up. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Joel, for our marketing project, I've chosen a real start-up, a company called Greenbottle, which sells reusable water bottles.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: I like that. What's their problem?

script.speaker: priya
script.text: They've only been going for a year, and they have almost no customers outside their home town. They've asked us to design a social media plan.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: Which platform should we concentrate on? There's so much choice.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: I'd say Instagram, because their product looks good in photographs, and the audience they want is young. TikTok is possible, but it takes a lot more time.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: Who is the main target audience? Families, or students?

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Students, mainly. They carry bottles all day, and they care about the environment. Families come second.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: What's wrong with their current posts?

script.speaker: priya
script.text: The photos are poor. They're dark and blurry, so it's the first thing we'd improve. The text is fine.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: How often should they post? Every day sounds like a lot.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Three times a week is realistic for a small company. More than that and the quality drops.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Let me describe the plan. First, the company should run a customer survey, to find out what people really want from a bottle.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: Then each week, they post a short video, showing the bottles in use, for example on a hike or in a gym.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: And they need to find local influencers, popular people with a lot of followers, and ask them to try the product.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: We should also create a campaign hashtag, so that customers can share their own photos, and the company can repost the best ones.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: And everything has to fit a small budget, because they only have a few hundred pounds a month.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: That's the main limit, so we'll need to say what to do first.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: I'll draw up the plan tonight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the Silk Road
parts.context: A history lecture on the network of trade routes.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the Silk Road. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today we're going to talk about the Silk Road, which was not a single road, but a huge network of trade routes that linked China with the Mediterranean for well over a thousand years.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Interestingly, the name is quite modern. It was invented in the nineteenth century by a German geographer, who wanted a simple name for these ancient routes. The people who used them never called them that.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The routes began to open in the second century BC, when the Han emperor sent an explorer called Zhang Qian to the west to look for allies. He returned with news of distant lands and fine horses, and the trade developed from there.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: It's a mistake to imagine merchants travelling from China to Rome. Most traders carried goods over short sections of the route, and sold them to the next merchant, so that a bale of silk passed through many hands. The goods included silk, jade, glass and spices, as well as horses and gold.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Travel was slow and dangerous. Caravans of camels crossed deserts and mountains, and rested at roadside inns called caravanserais, where merchants could find food, water and a safe place to store their goods.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Cities along the way grew rich. Samarkand and Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan, became great centres of trade and learning, where merchants from many countries met and exchanged not only goods but also ideas.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: For centuries the Chinese kept the secret of silk production, until about the sixth century, when monks smuggled silkworm eggs to the Byzantine Empire. And ideas travelled too. Buddhism spread from India to China, and paper and gunpowder travelled west.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The routes declined when sea routes opened in the fifteenth century, and it became cheaper to move goods by ship. Next week we'll look at the spice trade.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
